A.explanation: Two symmetric components in parallel would conduct for both positive and negative $V$, so current would not be zero in reverse.

B.explanation: Two symmetric components in series would still conduct for both directions of $V$, so it cannot give zero current for negative $V$.

C.explanation: In parallel the filament lamp branch would still carry current when the diode is in reverse bias, so reverse current would not be zero.

D.explanation: In series the diode blocks reverse current while the filament lamp makes the forward $I$-$V$ curve flatten as resistance rises with temperature.

hints: Look at the measured $I$ against $V$ graph: there is a rising curve with decreasing slope for $V > 0$ but $I$ stays at zero for $V < 0$.
Remember how a filament lamp $I$-$V$ bends over because heating increases resistance, and how a semiconductor diode passes current in forward bias but blocks it in reverse bias.
Ask what happens in reverse bias if the two components share the same current in series compared with having separate current paths in parallel.
walkthrough: Read the graph axes: $I$ is plotted vertically against $V$ horizontally. For $V > 0$ the current rises steeply then the slope decreases, and for $V < 0$ the current remains essentially zero.
Recall the component shapes: a filament lamp has a symmetric $I$-$V$ that curves to the $V$-axis at larger $|V|$ because $R = V/I$ increases as the filament gets hot.
Recall the diode shape: it conducts easily in the forward direction but passes almost no current in the reverse direction, giving a strongly asymmetric $I$-$V$.

Combine them with the same current through both: in forward bias both can conduct so the box shows the lamp-like rising and flattening curve, while in reverse bias the diode blocks the single series path so total $I$ is zero.
A parallel pair cannot do this because the non-diode branch would still conduct in reverse and give non-zero reverse $I$. This is option D
